title: Medicine enters the university

confidence.note: Universities grew up gradually, so there is no single founding date; Montpellier's 1220 statutes and 1289 papal bull are documented in later reference works. The 1322 case against Jacoba Felicie survives in the court records printed in the Paris university cartulary.

people: Cardinal Conrad, papal legate who gave Montpellier its 1220 statutes
Jacoba Felicie (fl. 1322), Paris healer prosecuted by the medical faculty
summary: In the 13th century medicine became a university subject. By 1322 the Paris faculty was prosecuting unlicensed healers, among them a woman her own patients praised.
body: Medicine was among the subjects taught in Europe's first universities. Bologna's grew up around student guilds, at first of law; at Paris, in the last quarter of the 12th century, masters of theology, law, medicine and arts joined in a single teaching body. At Montpellier, statutes given in 1220 by the papal legate Cardinal Conrad placed the medical school under the bishop of Maguelonne, and a papal bull of 1289 combined its schools into a university. Students learned from books, above all Galen and Avicenna, whose works Pope Clement V prescribed for Montpellier in 1309; practical anatomy followed the manuals of Mondino and Henri de Mondeville.

Faculties also used their licenses to police the market. In 1322 the Paris faculty prosecuted Jacoba Felicie, a woman her own pleading described as about thirty, for practicing without its approval, under a rule threatening excommunication and a fine of sixty Paris pounds. One patient testified that she had treated him better than physicians would have. She argued that it was better and more decent for a skilled woman to examine a sick woman than for a man to do so. The same prohibition was served on other women and men, among them a woman surgeon, Margaret of Ypres, and a Jewish woman, Belota.

title: Frederick II licenses doctors

confidence.note: The Constitutions of Melfi of 1231 survive and their medical clauses are well studied. How strictly the rules were enforced across the kingdom is not shown by the sources used here.

people: Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor and king of Sicily
summary: In 1231 Emperor Frederick II made medicine a regulated profession in southern Italy, with set studies, fee rules, and a wall between doctors and druggists.
body: In 1231, at Melfi, Emperor Frederick II issued a law code for his Kingdom of Sicily that devoted five constitutions to medicine. They fixed the course of study and the conditions for admission to practice, with the masters of Salerno at the center; William Osler summarized them as three years of preliminary study and five of medicine, surgery included. The laws set how often doctors should visit patients and what they could charge, and banned partnerships between physicians and apothecaries, who had to swear to make up prescriptions honestly. Surgeons needed proof of a year's study, including human anatomy.

title: The invention of spectacles

confidence.note: Sources place the invention in the late 13th century: one reading of Giordano's 1306 sermon gives c. 1290, one modern study says shortly after 1286, and Venetian guild rules mention eyeglasses by about 1300. Who and where are unsettled: a Pisan chronicle credits Alessandro della Spina but says he copied an unnamed earlier maker, and the Enciclopedia Italiana favors an unknown Venetian glassmaker.

people: Giordano da Pisa (also called Giordano da Rivalto), Dominican preacher
Alessandro della Spina (d. by 1313), Dominican friar of Pisa
summary: Around 1290 someone in northern Italy joined two lenses with a rivet and gave aging readers back their eyes. Nobody knows who, and the famous Florentine claimant is a forgery.
body: Eyeglasses appeared in northern Italy in the late 13th century, and no one knows who made the first pair. One modern study puts them shortly after 1286, most likely in Pisa. A sermon of 1306 by the Dominican preacher Giordano da Pisa is read by the Italian national biographical dictionary as dating the first pair, made by his fellow friar Alessandro della Spina, to around 1290. The chronicle of their convent, Santa Caterina in Pisa, says only that Alessandro made and shared eyeglasses that someone else had made first and would not share. The Enciclopedia Italiana prefers Venice: guild rules from the end of the 13th century mention eyeglasses as distinct from reading stones, and it reports the widely accepted view that an unknown Venetian glassmaker invented them. By 1300 Venetian glassmakers were certainly producing eyeglasses.

The first spectacles were two convex lenses in frames riveted together at the handles, clamped on the nose and often steadied by hand. They helped the farsighted read, which suited the few who lived past their forties and could read at all. Lenses for the nearsighted, harder to grind, arrived only in the mid-15th century.

myth.tradition: Spectacles were invented by Salvino degli Armati of Florence, whose tomb in Santa Maria Maggiore supposedly called him 'inventor of eyeglasses' and who was honored with a monument there in the 19th century.
myth.record: The epitaph, supposedly dated 1318, is known only from Ferdinando Leopoldo del Migliore's 1684 history of Florence, which said it came from an old burial register. The historian Isidoro del Lungo showed in 1920 how false notices and false inscriptions had built the identification of Salvino; the Enciclopedia Italiana calls the claim sheer mystification.

links.note: Optical theory of the age; Roger Bacon discussed magnifying lenses but is not credited with spectacles.

title: Mondino dissects in Bologna

confidence.note: Sources agree the Anathomia was written in 1316, and its use for about two centuries is well documented. Whether Mondino wielded the knife himself or read while an assistant cut is still debated.

people: Mondino de' Liuzzi (born c. 1270–1275, died 1326), Bolognese physician and anatomist
summary: In 1316 a Bologna professor wrote the dissection manual that Europe's medical schools relied on for the next two centuries.
body: Bologna was already opening bodies before Mondino de' Liuzzi: from 1265 the city had a body of physicians who examined corpses in cases of fatal wounds. Mondino, a pupil of Taddeo Alderotti, made dissection an accepted part of teaching. In 1316 he finished his *Anathomia*, a short manual organized in the order a body has to be opened before it decays. He mentions anatomizing a woman in January 1316 and refers to dissections of nearly monthly frequency, on executed criminals, presumably on the hospital poor, and on pigs. The book was used in Europe's medical schools until the mid-16th century.

Its anatomy was mostly Galen's and the Arabic writers', errors included: a five-lobed liver taken from dogs and a womb with seven chambers. The book's style suggests it was meant to be read aloud while others worked; illustrations from the later 14th century show a professor reading from a book on a platform, a demonstrator pointing, and a dissector, a barber or surgeon, cutting. Mondino could learn, though. By 1319, having read a new Latin translation of Galen's *On the Use of Parts*, he dropped the seven-chambered womb.

myth.tradition: Mondino's dissector was a young woman, Alessandra Giliani, remembered as a pioneering female anatomist.
myth.record: The story took hold in 1739, when the Bolognese historian Alessandro Macchiavelli passed off the long-haired dissector in an image in a 15th-century edition of Mondino's text as Alessandra Giliani, backing the claim with fake sources. It was believed for more than two centuries.

title: The Black Death

confidence.note: Chronicles, tax records and burial grounds date the pandemic's spread across Europe closely, and ancient DNA has settled that the killer was Yersinia pestis. The death toll is an estimate from patchy records: recent studies quote anything from 30% to 60%, and the Central Asian origin rests on a single 2022 study of seven individuals, of whom three yielded plague DNA.

place: Central Eurasia to Europe, the Middle East and North Africa
people: Maria Spyrou, geneticist, lead author of the 2022 origin study
Philip VI, king of France, who commissioned the Paris report
summary: Between 1346 and 1353 plague killed perhaps a third to more than half of the people it reached. Ancient DNA now points to a source near a lake in Kyrgyzstan.
body: In 1338 and 1339 an epidemic devastated a trading community near Lake Issyk-Kul, in what is now Kyrgyzstan. Its tombstones, inscribed in Syriac, give the cause of death as "pestilence." In 2022 a team led by Maria Spyrou sampled teeth from seven people excavated there between 1885 and 1892; three showed signs of plague DNA, and two genomes were reconstructed. That strain of *Yersinia pestis* is the most recent common ancestor of the great diversification of plague lineages linked to the pandemic's emergence, and comparison with present-day strains from the Tian Shan region supports a local origin. One of the most popular earlier theories had placed the source in China.

Plague first entered the Mediterranean in 1347, on trade ships carrying goods from the Golden Horde's territories on the Black Sea, and between 1346 and 1353 it swept through Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. How many died is still argued over: recent studies estimate up to 30–50% of the population, while others say up to 60%. For decades the cause itself was debated, and early ancient-DNA results were controversial. In 2010 a team reported *Yersinia pestis* DNA from plague pits in England, France and the Netherlands, and plague protein from pits in Italy and Germany too; a full medieval genome from a London cemetery followed in 2011.

People explained the catastrophe with the best science they had. In October 1348 the medical masters of Paris, writing at the command of King Philip, named a "distant and first cause": a conjunction of three planets in Aquarius at one hour after noon on 20 March 1345, which had corrupted the air. Astrology and bad air were mainstream natural philosophy, not superstition. Others found human culprits. Jews were accused of poisoning wells, tortured into confessions and killed across Germany; in Strasbourg on 14 February 1349 about two thousand were burned on a wooden platform in their own cemetery.

Medicine had no answer. Guy de Chauliac, the pope's physician at Avignon, wrote that the mortality "rendered doctors useless." Some of the lasting responses, such as quarantine, would be administrative rather than medical. The Black Death was only the first wave of a second plague pandemic that kept returning for some 500 years, into the early 19th century.

title: Quarantine is invented

confidence.note: The Ragusan ordinance is preserved in the council's register, the Liber viridis, and is dated 27 July 1377. That it is the earliest known quarantine rests on Mirko Grmek's work of the late 1970s as summarized by Ravančić; Ravančić judges the measures effective, since Ragusa had no major plague outbreak until 1391.

people: Mirko Dražen Grmek, Croatian physician and historian of medicine who showed Dubrovnik's priority
summary: In 1377 the Adriatic port of Ragusa made travelers from plague zones wait a month before entering. Venice later stretched it to forty days and gave the world a word.
body: On 27 July 1377 the Great Council of Ragusa, a trading republic on the Adriatic, passed an ordinance whose title states the rule: *Veniens de locis pestiferis non intret Ragusinum vel districtum*, whoever comes from plague-stricken places shall not enter Ragusa or its territory. Arrivals had to spend a month in isolation first. Townspeople who visited them, or brought them food without authorization, had to stay a month too. Earlier cities had expelled or walled up the sick; in 1348 Milan's archbishop had the first three plague houses boarded up with everyone inside. Ragusa's isolation was temporary, which kept the port open to trade. As far as can be told, the councillors did not consult the city's physicians and had no medical theory of contagion, only hard experience.

The system grew. Ragusa set up a standing health office by 1397, and Venice opened the first permanent plague hospital, or lazaretto, on the island of Santa Maria di Nazareth in 1423. In the mid-15th century Venice lengthened the wait from 30 to 40 days, *quaranta*, which gave quarantine its name.

myth.record: Venice gave quarantine its 40-day length and its name, but the earliest known ordinance imposing temporary isolation on arrivals is Ragusa's of 1377, as Mirko Grmek showed in the late 1970s.

title: Guy de Chauliac's Great Surgery

confidence.note: The completion date of 1363 is given consistently by historians, and Guy's own words survive in his book. His birth and death dates are less certain, given variously as c. 1290–1300 and 1368–1370.

people: Guy de Chauliac (born c. 1290–1300, died c. 1368–1370), surgeon and papal physician
summary: The pope's physician stayed in plague-stricken Avignon, caught the disease, survived, and wrote the surgical textbook Europe used for three centuries.
body: When plague reached Avignon in January 1348, Guy de Chauliac, educated at Montpellier and Bologna, was physician to Pope Clement VI. He wrote that doctors dared not visit the sick, and that he himself, "in order to avoid a bad reputation," did not dare leave. Late in the outbreak he caught the disease and lay ill for nearly six weeks with a swelling in his groin. In 1363 he finished his *Chirurgia magna* (Great Surgery), blending Greek and Arabic authorities with his own experience, including ways of tying off bleeding vessels. Translated into several vernaculars, among them Middle English, it remained a standard surgical text for three centuries.

links.note: His eyewitness account of the plague at Avignon.
